questions.q: In the sudoers fix for lnx-app-02, why is the appsvc account granted `NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart meridian-app` instead of a wildcard `ALL`?
options: NOPASSWD entries are required by sudoers syntax for every account
Wildcard grants are no longer supported in modern sudo versions
Sudo access should be scoped to exactly the commands a role needs, not a blanket grant that lets the account run anything as root
It has no real security benefit, it's purely stylistic
questions.explain: The leftover wildcard entry let the service account run anything as root — scoping it to one command is the actual fix.

questions.q: Why does this lab run `ausearch -m avc -ts recent` before running `setenforce 1`?
options: To check for existing SELinux denials first, so enforcing mode doesn't immediately break the running application
To generate new denials for testing purposes
To disable SELinux permanently before enforcing
Because setenforce requires a prior audit log entry to run at all
questions.explain: Checking for denials and fixing mislabeled contexts first prevents enforcing mode from breaking a live application the moment it goes active.

questions.q: What does setting `PasswordAuthentication no` in sshd_config accomplish, alongside `PermitRootLogin no`?
options: It disables SSH entirely on the server
It only affects root logins, not other accounts
It removes the password fallback entirely, so SSH access only works with a valid key — there's no weaker path in if a key is misplaced
It has no effect unless fail2ban is also installed
questions.explain: With password authentication off, there's no fallback login method weaker than key-based auth for any account on the server.

questions.q: In the fail2ban jail configured here (`maxretry = 4`, `findtime = 10m`, `bantime = 1h`), what triggers a ban?
options: Four failed login attempts from the same address within a ten-minute window
Four successful logins in a row
A ban only triggers after a manual review
Any single failed login attempt
questions.explain: Fail2ban counts failed attempts within the findtime window and bans once maxretry is reached, here for one hour.

questions.q: Why are the auditd rules in this lab tagged with keys like `identity` and `privilege_escalation`?
options: Tags disable logging for all other files
So a search like `ausearch -k privilege_escalation` can quickly surface exactly the relevant events an audit is looking for
The tags are required by auditd syntax and have no functional purpose
Tags determine which files get backed up automatically
questions.explain: Keys let an admin or auditor filter audit search results to exactly the category of change they're investigating.
